full_judgment:
In this Rule the petitioner has challenged a decision of the lover appellate court reversing a decision of the trial court in pre-emption case under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Initially the pre-emption case was instituted at the instance of a contiguous owner. Upon service of notice to all the co-sharers, a co-sharer by inheritance was also made a co-applicant in the pre-emption case. Thus, both a contiguous owner and a co-sharer were claiming pre-emption of the self same land. The trial court allowed the pre-emption claimed by the contiguous owner and disallowed the claim of the co-sharer on the ground that it was time barred. The lower appellate court did just the opposite by allowing the pre-emption in favour of the co-sharer and disallowing it against the contiguous owner. While doing so, the lower appellate court came to a finding of fact on consideration of the evidence on record and in the facts and circumstances of the case that the claim of the co-sharer for pre-emption was made within the statutory period of 4 months from the date of the personal knowledge of the co-sharer about the impugned transfer and such finding of fact made by the lower appellate court in the absence of any apparent error of law on the face of the record is otherwise conclusive. In this connection it may be mentioned that the lower appellate court did not reverse the finding of the trial court about the filing of the pre-emption case by a contiguous owner within the statutory period of limitation of 4 months from the date of the knowledge of the impugned transfer. 

 2. The only question for determination in this Rule is thus as to who will have priority in claiming pre-emption in between a co-sharer and a contiguous owner. Sub-section (1) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act providing for a right of pre-emption has mentioned a co-sharer in the first instance and subsequently a contiguous owner has been added. From the reading of section 96 (1) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act it would clearly appear that the co-sharer comes first in priority over a contiguous owner. Further, a co-sharer can always be divided into co-sharer by inheritance and co-sharer by purchase. Even if it is assumed that a co-sharer by inheritance or purchase and a contiguous owner are put on the same footing for the purpose of enabling any of them to claim pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, upon a clear equitable principle a co-sharer by inheritance shall have the highest priority followed by a co-sharer by purchase and thereafter a contiguous owner. The very purpose of granting pre-emption to avoid any stranger in any joint holding or neighbourhood would be frustrated if such priority as held herein before is not maintained for ends of justice.
